title: It speaks like an adult before it speaks like a child
body: #1 has lived its first 72 months. Before it heard anything it produced random characters. At 12 months it already strings real words together, and from then on it talks in whole adult sentences: asked “do you want to play with the ball?”, the 18-month snapshot answers “we wanted to play with you today”.

Real children are nowhere near this. Counting only real words, #1 at 12 months says 3.5 words per utterance; children of the same age in the same recordings say 0.9. At 18 months it is 4.4 against 1.5; at 36 months 5.0 against 3.4.

The reason is how it was raised. It only ever heard adults talking to children, so the first thing it learns to imitate is an adult. The short, telegraphic speech of a two-year-old does not grow out of learning from this input alone. Whatever produces it — a body, a world, a mind that cannot yet hold a long sentence — is missing from #1.

title: The first copy
body: The lineage starts by copying. Grown #1 copies, word by word, everything adults said to children in its own upbringing. At each word it lapses with probability 5% and writes the word it expects instead of the one in front of it. Its copy will raise the next generation.

In a first test on 800 lines, 82% came through unchanged. A lapse is the parent's own guess, so it leans towards what the parent expects: rare words often turn into common ones (“ball” became “beautiful”, “telephones” became “and”), and agreement can shift (“when are you gonna bring em home” became “when is you gonna bring em home”). Whether these drifts pile up over generations is what the lineage is for.

correction: Correction (see 20261028-03): on the full copy, “rare words often turn into common ones” does not hold beyond what any word swap would do. The examples were picked from a small test.

title: Correction: the lapses do not favour common words
body: The full first copy is done: 800,527 lines, 82% unchanged, 180,335 lapses. Entry 20261028-02 said that a lapse leans towards common words. That came from a handful of examples, and it does not survive a fair comparison.

The comparison is a null model: at every lapse, instead of letting #1 write a word, draw a word at random by how often it occurs in the original. Any swap pulls a rare word towards commoner ones, simply because most words drawn are common; that is regression to the mean, not a property of the copyist.

Measured against this null, #1 pulls rare words upward slightly less than random swapping does, and pulls frequent words downward slightly less too. Its replacements stay closer to the frequency of the word they replace. What #1 does at a lapse looks more like finding a word that fits the context than like reaching for a common one. It also invented 7,479 non-words.

title: A slip the next generation repeats? (a hint, not a finding)
body: #4, #5 and #6 are grown. They are the first children of the lineage: same learner and same upbringing as #1, #2 and #3, same seeds, but instead of the original recordings they heard #1's copy of them, in which 5% of words were written #1's own way.

Some of #1's lapses broke agreement between subject and verb: “when are you gonna bring em home” became “when is you gonna bring em home”. Phrases like “are he” do not occur in the original at all; #1's copy has 14 of them.

When the children speak, these mismatches turn up a little more often than in their parents' generation. #4 says “where are he going” and “what are he doing”. Over all the speech each generation produced (about 58,000 utterances per individual), “are he” appears 15 times in the children against 5 in the parents, “is we” 13 against 4, “are it” 7 against 2.

This is a hint, not a result. The counts are tiny, some matches are ordinary sentences, and there is no comparison yet with a null model or with a second generation. The real test comes when #4 copies the book it grew up with: if the mismatches it learned make its own lapses lean the same way, the slip has started to spread.
